children: Bitcoin options traders are buying puts at a pace not seen since the 2022 capitulation. That is a signal of extreme bearishness, and the market data backs it up.
The most crowded bet on Deribit right now is not a moonshot call. It is the $60,000 put, carrying a notional value of approximately $900 million in open interest.
A put option is basically an insurance policy. You pay a premium for the right to sell Bitcoin at a set price, which pays off if the market falls below it.
The $60,000 strike on Deribit climbed to the top of the open interest rankings in mid-to-late November. It overtook the $100,000 call, which had previously held the top spot.
The trigger was a sharp sell-off. Bitcoin fell approximately 12% heading into mid-November, sinking to four-month lows around $62,000 before recovering part of the drop.
Activity was not limited to the screen-traded market. Block trades in puts topped $1 billion, with Paradigm, a venue for large negotiated trades, seeing particularly heavy flow.

A single trader stood out. As spot prices fell, this participant kept rolling put positions down to lower strikes, a process that involves closing existing contracts and reopening them at new price levels.
The strikes slid from $74,000 in late October to $63,000.
Volatility told a similar story. Deribit's Bitcoin implied volatility index, known as BVIV, peaked at 57.13 on November 15-16 before cooling off.
The put-to-call open interest ratio on Deribit sat between 0.81 and 0.91 in late November. Very short-dated contracts showed higher readings.
That detail adds some nuance. A ratio below 1 means calls still outnumber puts overall, but the gap has narrowed, and the near-term action is leaning defensive.
The derivatives market was not alone in its caution. US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded approximately $1.07 billion in net outflows during the week leading up to November 13.
Those funds are a key channel for institutional and retail money that prefers a brokerage account to a crypto exchange. When that pipe runs in reverse, it removes a source of steady buying pressure.

The first takeaway is that positioning has turned decisively toward risk management. The largest open interest strike sitting at $60,000 suggests a meaningful share of the market sees further downside as a real possibility, not a tail risk.

Spot at around $62,000 at its recent low was uncomfortably close to that strike. Any renewed slide toward $60,000 would test how much of that put demand is hedging versus outright bearish speculation.
The easing in implied volatility after the November 15-16 peak is also worth noting. Fear spiked, then cooled somewhat as Bitcoin bounced off its lows.

For investors, the signals to track are fairly clear. Watch whether ETF flows stabilize after the approximately $1.07 billion weekly outflow, whether the put-to-call ratio climbs toward or above 1, and whether the large trader on Paradigm keeps rolling strikes lower.

title: Bitcoin options traders pile into puts at a pace last seen in 2022
